course.title: Ancient Greece: History & Civilization
course.description: A guided survey of ancient Greek history from the Bronze Age palaces of Crete to the Hellenistic kingdoms that followed Alexander the Great. You will trace the rise of the polis, the rivalry of Athens and Sparta, the Persian Wars, the Golden Age, and the ideas in philosophy, science, and art that still shape the modern world. Structure and facts are adapted from the Ancient Greece article on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: Which island was the center of the Minoan civilization, the earliest in the Greek world?
questions.explanation: The Minoans flourished on Crete, where their great palace at Knossos stood.

questions.prompt: Whose reforms of 508 BCE are usually credited with establishing Athenian democracy?
questions.explanation: Cleisthenes reorganized the citizen body in 508 BCE and is called the father of Athenian democracy.

questions.prompt: At which 490 BCE battle did the Athenians defeat the first Persian invasion?
questions.explanation: Athens won at Marathon in 490 BCE, repelling the invasion sent by Darius I.

questions.prompt: Who was the teacher of Plato?
questions.explanation: Socrates taught Plato, who in turn taught Aristotle.

questions.prompt: The Olympic Games were traditionally first held in which year?
questions.explanation: The first recorded Olympic Games were in 776 BCE at Olympia, held every four years.

questions.prompt: The Peloponnesian War (431 to 404 BCE) was fought mainly between Athens and which rival?
questions.explanation: The war pitted Athens and its naval empire against Sparta and its land-based alliance.

questions.prompt: Alexander the Great came from which kingdom to the north of Greece?
questions.explanation: Alexander was king of Macedon, whose army had already mastered Greece under his father Philip II.

questions.prompt: The Parthenon, built in the 5th century BCE, was a temple dedicated to which deity?
questions.explanation: The Parthenon on the Acropolis honored Athena, the patron goddess of Athens.

lessons.title: Minoans, Mycenaeans, and the Greek Dark Ages
lessons.grammar_note: Dates before the year 1 are written BCE and count downward, so 1450 BCE is earlier than 1100 BCE.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Place the first Greek civilizations in order and explain how Bronze Age Greece collapsed and slowly recovered. By the end you will be able to name the Minoan and Mycenaean cultures, say roughly when each flourished, describe what archaeologists found at Knossos and Mycenae, and explain why the period after 1100 BCE is called the Greek Dark Ages. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which island was the heart of the earliest of these civilizations, and what later culture rose on the Greek mainland? Keep those two names in mind, because the whole story of early Greece is the handoff from one to the other and then the long silence that followed before the Greek world learned to write again. Getting this foundation firm will make every later lesson, from the polis to Alexander, far easier to follow.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Greek history opens on Crete with the Minoan civilization, which flourished from about 3000 to 1450 BCE. The Minoans built sprawling palace complexes, the largest at Knossos, decorated with bright frescoes of dolphins, bulls, and athletes. They wrote in a script called Linear A that has never been deciphered, and they traded across the eastern Mediterranean. Around 1600 BCE a volcanic eruption on the island of Thera disrupted the region, and by about 1450 BCE Minoan power faded. On the mainland the Mycenaean civilization rose, roughly 1600 to 1100 BCE, centered on fortified citadels such as Mycenae, Pylos, and Tiryns. The Mycenaeans were warlike kings who wrote an early form of Greek in Linear B, a script that has been read. Around 1200 to 1100 BCE this Bronze Age world collapsed across the region, and the palaces were abandoned. What followed, roughly 1100 to 800 BCE, is the Greek Dark Ages: writing was lost, trade shrank, and population fell, until a gradual recovery set the stage for classical Greece.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: Knossos: the great Minoan palace on Crete, excavated by Arthur Evans starting in 1900 CE, who named the culture after the legendary King Minos. Linear A and Linear B: the Minoan and Mycenaean scripts; Linear B was deciphered as Greek by Michael Ventris in 1952 CE, while Linear A remains unread. Thera eruption (about the 1600s BCE): a massive volcanic blast that damaged Minoan sites and later fed myths of a lost world. Mycenae: the mainland citadel with its Lion Gate and shaft graves full of gold, tied in legend to King Agamemnon of the Trojan War. Bronze Age collapse (about 1200 to 1100 BCE): a wave of destruction across the eastern Mediterranean that toppled the Mycenaean palaces. Greek Dark Ages (about 1100 to 800 BCE): centuries with no written records. Around 800 BCE the Greeks adapted the Phoenician alphabet to write their own language, and the poems of Homer, the Iliad and the Odyssey, were composed and later written down, marking the end of the silence.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which civilization came first, the Minoan or the Mycenaean? 2) Name the largest Minoan palace. 3) Which of the two scripts, Linear A or Linear B, has been deciphered? 4) Roughly when did the Bronze Age collapse occur? 5) From where did the Greeks borrow the alphabet around 800 BCE? 6) Which two epic poems mark the recovery from the Dark Ages? Answers: 1) The Minoan (about 3000 to 1450 BCE) came before the Mycenaean (about 1600 to 1100 BCE). 2) Knossos, on Crete. 3) Linear B, read as an early form of Greek. 4) About 1200 to 1100 BCE. 5) From the Phoenicians, whose alphabet the Greeks adapted by adding vowels. 6) The Iliad and the Odyssey, attributed to Homer.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: mixing up the Minoans and the Mycenaeans. Remember the Minoans were on the island of Crete and came first; the Mycenaeans were on the mainland and came second. Mistake: assuming the Dark Ages were totally empty. They were poorer and had no writing, but communities survived and iron-working spread. Mistake: calling Linear A readable; only Linear B has been deciphered. A final caution: the eruption of Thera weakened the Minoans but did not instantly destroy them, and the Trojan War is legend layered over Mycenaean memory, not a documented event. Exit ticket: (a) On which island did the Minoan civilization develop? (b) What single technology, lost in the collapse, returned around 800 BCE and ended the Dark Ages? Answers: (a) Crete. (b) Writing, as the Greeks adopted an alphabet from the Phoenicians.

lessons.title: The polis, colonization, Athens, and Sparta
lessons.grammar_note: The word 'politics' comes from 'polis'; many English terms, from 'democracy' to 'tyranny', are Greek in origin.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what a polis was, why Greeks founded colonies across the Mediterranean, and how the two most famous city-states, Athens and Sparta, differed in the deepest way. By the end you will be able to define the polis, list a few reasons for colonization, outline the steps by which Athens built its democracy, and describe the military society of Sparta. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, whose reforms of 508 BCE are usually said to have founded Athenian democracy? Hold that name, because Athens and Sparta answered the same question, how should a community govern itself, in opposite ways, and that contrast drives much of the rest of Greek history. Thinking about why one city trusted ordinary citizens with power while the other trained them for war will make every later conflict easier to understand.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: After the Dark Ages the basic unit of Greek life became the polis, or city-state: an independent town with its surrounding farmland, its own laws, army, and gods. There were hundreds of them, fiercely proud and often at war. Because Greece is mountainous and its soil thin, growing populations pushed Greeks overseas. From about 750 to 550 BCE they founded colonies around the Mediterranean and Black Sea, from Massalia in the west to the shores of Asia Minor and southern Italy, so many in Italy and Sicily that the region was called Magna Graecia, Greater Greece. Each polis governed itself in its own way. Athens moved step by step toward democracy: Draco wrote harsh laws in 621 BCE, Solon eased debt and widened participation in 594 BCE, and Cleisthenes reorganized the citizen body in 508 BCE, giving rise to rule by the demos, the people. Sparta took the opposite path. It turned its whole free population into a professional army, supported by a huge enslaved workforce, and prized discipline, obedience, and military excellence above all.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: Polis: the self-governing Greek city-state, the setting for Greek politics (a word that comes from polis itself). Colonization (about 750 to 550 BCE): waves of settlement that spread Greek language and culture across the Mediterranean. Draco (621 BCE): an Athenian lawgiver whose code was so severe we still call harsh rules draconian. Solon (594 BCE): reformer who canceled debts and opened offices by wealth rather than birth. Cleisthenes (508 BCE): the father of Athenian democracy, who reorganized citizens into ten tribes and strengthened the assembly. In Athens free adult male citizens voted directly in the assembly, though women, enslaved people, and foreigners were excluded. Sparta: a society of two hereditary kings, a council of elders, and five annually elected ephors, where boys entered the agoge military training at age seven. The Spartans ruled over the helots, an enslaved population many times their number, which is why they kept such a formidable standing army. Lycurgus is the legendary lawgiver credited with this whole system.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is a polis? 2) Name the region of southern Italy and Sicily so heavily settled it was called Greater Greece. 3) Which Athenian reformer of 508 BCE is called the father of democracy? 4) Who could actually vote in the Athenian assembly? 5) At what age did a Spartan boy begin military training? 6) What was the name of the enslaved population that supported Sparta? Answers: 1) An independent Greek city-state with its own laws, army, and gods. 2) Magna Graecia. 3) Cleisthenes. 4) Free adult male citizens; women, enslaved people, and foreigners were excluded. 5) Age seven, when he entered the agoge. 6) The helots.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: imagining Greece as one country. It was hundreds of rival city-states that shared a language and religion but almost never a single government. Mistake: calling Athenian democracy universal. It was direct but narrow, limited to free adult male citizens, so most people living in Athens could not vote. Mistake: confusing the reformers; Solon came in 594 BCE and eased debt, while Cleisthenes came later in 508 BCE and built the democratic structure. Mistake: picturing Sparta as an ordinary kingdom; it had two kings at once and real power lay with the ephors and the assembly of soldiers. Exit ticket: (a) Which city-state is famous for direct democracy, and which for its military society? (b) Who did the work that freed Spartan men to train full time for war? Answers: (a) Athens for democracy, Sparta for its military society. (b) The helots, Sparta's enslaved population.

lessons.title: The Persian Wars: Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis
lessons.grammar_note: When two events share a year, note land versus sea or cause versus effect to keep them straight; Thermopylae and Salamis both fall in 480 BCE.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Narrate the Persian Wars in order and explain why a few Greek city-states managed to repel the largest empire of their day. By the end you will be able to place Marathon, Thermopylae, and Salamis in sequence, name the Persian kings and Greek leaders involved, and say why these victories mattered for the confidence of the Greek world. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, at which 490 BCE battle did the Athenians stop the first Persian invasion? Keep that battle in mind as the opening act. The Persian Wars are the moment when the quarrelsome city-states, briefly, fought on the same side, and the outcome made the Golden Age of Athens possible, so it is worth getting the sequence firmly in your head before moving on to the age that followed.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The Persian Empire, the superpower of the age, clashed with the Greeks in two great invasions. Trouble began with the Ionian Revolt of 499 to 494 BCE, when Greek cities in Asia Minor rose against Persian rule with Athenian help. In revenge, King Darius I launched the first invasion, which ended in 490 BCE at Marathon, where the heavily outnumbered Athenians, led by Miltiades, won a stunning victory on the plain northeast of Athens. Ten years later Darius's son Xerxes returned with a vast army and fleet. In 480 BCE a small Greek force under the Spartan king Leonidas held the narrow pass at Thermopylae for three days before being overwhelmed, buying time for the rest of Greece. That same year the Athenian statesman Themistocles lured the Persian navy into the narrow straits of Salamis and destroyed it. The following year, 479 BCE, the Greeks crushed the remaining Persian land army at Plataea, ending the threat for good.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: Ionian Revolt (499 to 494 BCE): the uprising of Greek cities in Asia Minor that provoked Persia. Darius I: the Persian king who sent the first invasion. Marathon (490 BCE): the Athenian victory under Miltiades; legend says a runner carried the news to Athens, the root of the modern race. Xerxes I: Darius's son, who led the massive second invasion in 480 BCE. Thermopylae (480 BCE): the pass where King Leonidas and a small force, including his famous 300 Spartans, fought to the death to delay the Persians. Salamis (480 BCE): the naval battle where Themistocles trapped and smashed the Persian fleet in narrow waters. Plataea (479 BCE): the decisive land battle that ended the invasion. Herodotus, often called the father of history, wrote the main surviving account of these wars. Remember the order within 480 BCE: Thermopylae and Salamis came in the same year, the first a delaying defeat on land, the second a victory at sea.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which revolt beginning in 499 BCE helped trigger the wars? 2) At which 490 BCE battle did Athens defeat Darius's first invasion? 3) Who led the Spartans at Thermopylae in 480 BCE? 4) Which Athenian leader engineered the naval victory at Salamis? 5) Which 479 BCE battle finally ended the Persian threat? 6) Which historian is our main source and is called the father of history? 7) Thermopylae and Salamis happened in which year? Answers: 1) The Ionian Revolt. 2) Marathon. 3) King Leonidas. 4) Themistocles. 5) Plataea. 6) Herodotus. 7) Both in 480 BCE, the first a land defeat, the second a naval victory.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: scrambling the order. The sequence is Ionian Revolt (499 to 494 BCE), then Marathon (490 BCE) under Darius, then Thermopylae and Salamis (both 480 BCE) under Xerxes, then Plataea (479 BCE). Mistake: thinking Thermopylae was a Greek win; it was a heroic defeat that bought time, and the war-deciding victories were Salamis at sea and Plataea on land. Mistake: assuming Sparta won Salamis; that was an Athenian-led naval triumph, while Sparta's stand came at Thermopylae. Mistake: believing all Greeks united; many city-states stayed neutral or even sided with Persia, and the alliance was fragile. Exit ticket: (a) Name the two 480 BCE battles and say which was on land and which at sea. (b) Which battle in 479 BCE ended the Persian invasions? Answers: (a) Thermopylae on land (a defeat) and Salamis at sea (a victory). (b) Plataea.

questions.prompt: Which civilization, centered on the island of Crete, came first?
questions.explanation: The Minoans (about 3000 to 1450 BCE) preceded the mainland Mycenaeans.

questions.prompt: The Greek Dark Ages followed the Bronze Age collapse around which period?
questions.explanation: The collapse came around 1200 to 1100 BCE, opening the Dark Ages that lasted until about 800 BCE.

questions.prompt: Which Athenian reformer is credited with founding democracy in 508 BCE?
questions.explanation: Cleisthenes reorganized the citizen body in 508 BCE; Solon and Draco came earlier.

questions.prompt: What was the enslaved population that supported the Spartan military system?
questions.explanation: The helots farmed the land so Spartan men could train for war full time.

questions.prompt: At which 490 BCE battle did Athens defeat the first Persian invasion?
questions.explanation: Athens won at Marathon in 490 BCE under Miltiades.

questions.prompt: In 480 BCE, in which naval battle did Themistocles destroy the Persian fleet?
questions.explanation: At Salamis, Themistocles lured the Persian navy into narrow straits and smashed it.

lessons.title: The Golden Age of Athens: Pericles, the Parthenon, and drama
lessons.grammar_note: Tragedy and comedy both began as Greek religious festivals honoring Dionysus; 'theater', 'drama', and 'chorus' are all Greek words.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the Golden Age of Athens and explain what made the mid-400s BCE such a creative high point. By the end you will be able to say who Pericles was, explain how the Delian League funded Athenian greatness, describe the Parthenon and who built it, and name the great playwrights and historians of the age. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, to which goddess was the Parthenon dedicated? Keep her in mind as you walk up to the temple in your imagination. This was the generation that turned a war-weary city into the cultural capital of the Greek world, and nearly everything we picture when we think of classical Greece, white marble temples, open-air theaters, and public debate, comes from these few remarkable decades centered on one dominant statesman.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: After the Persian Wars, Athens led the Delian League, an alliance formed in 478 BCE to guard against Persia. Athens gradually turned the league into an empire and moved its treasury to the city, using the funds to rebuild and beautify Athens. The leading statesman of the era was Pericles, dominant from about 461 to 429 BCE, who championed both democracy and a grand building program. Its crown was the Parthenon, a marble temple to Athena built on the Acropolis between 447 and 432 BCE, designed by the architects Ictinus and Callicrates and overseen by the sculptor Phidias. These were also the decades that perfected Greek drama, performed at festivals of Dionysus: the tragedians Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides, and the comic playwright Aristophanes. History-writing matured too, with Herodotus and then Thucydides, who recorded the war that would soon end this golden moment. It was an age of confidence, public art, and open argument, paid for, uncomfortably, by the tribute of Athens's allies.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: Delian League (founded 478 BCE): the anti-Persian alliance Athens led and then dominated, its treasury moved to Athens in 454 BCE. Pericles (about 495 to 429 BCE): the statesman whose name the era bears; he widened democracy by paying citizens for public service and drove the building program. Parthenon (447 to 432 BCE): the Doric temple of Athena on the Acropolis, with sculptures by Phidias and architecture by Ictinus and Callicrates. Greek tragedy: Aeschylus (the Oresteia), Sophocles (Oedipus Rex, Antigone), and Euripides (Medea) competed at the festival of Dionysus. Comedy: Aristophanes mocked politicians and ideas in plays such as The Clouds and Lysistrata. Herodotus wrote the history of the Persian Wars; Thucydides wrote a rigorous, eyewitness history of the Peloponnesian War. Together these figures gave the world enduring models of architecture, theater, and historical writing, all within a single remarkable lifetime centered on Periclean Athens.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which alliance, formed in 478 BCE, did Athens turn into an empire? 2) Which statesman led Athens during its Golden Age? 3) On which hill, and to which goddess, was the Parthenon built? 4) In roughly which years was the Parthenon constructed? 5) Name one of the three great tragedians. 6) Which historian wrote a careful account of the Peloponnesian War? Answers: 1) The Delian League. 2) Pericles. 3) On the Acropolis, dedicated to Athena. 4) Between 447 and 432 BCE. 5) Aeschylus, Sophocles, or Euripides. 6) Thucydides.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: imagining the Golden Age was funded purely by Athenian wealth. Much of it came from tribute paid by the Delian League's members, whom Athens treated as subjects. Mistake: confusing the playwrights; the three tragedians are Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides, while Aristophanes wrote comedy. Mistake: mixing up the historians; Herodotus covered the Persian Wars, Thucydides the Peloponnesian War. Mistake: thinking the Parthenon honored Zeus; it was the temple of Athena, the city's patron goddess. One more caution: the Golden Age was brief, and the same empire that paid for it provoked the war that would end it. Exit ticket: (a) Who was the leading statesman of the Athenian Golden Age? (b) To which goddess was the Parthenon dedicated, and on which hill does it stand? Answers: (a) Pericles. (b) Athena, on the Acropolis.

lessons.title: Philosophy, religion, myth, and the Olympic Games
lessons.grammar_note: The Olympic four-year cycle was called an Olympiad, and the Greeks used it to count years much as we count from a fixed point.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain the birth of Greek philosophy and the shape of Greek religion, and say why the Olympic Games mattered. By the end you will be able to place Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle in order as teacher and student, describe the Twelve Olympian gods and the oracle at Delphi, and date the first Olympic Games. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, who was the teacher of Plato, and in which year were the Olympics traditionally first held? Keep both facts handy. This lesson gathers the Greek life of the mind and spirit: the philosophers who asked how we should live and what we can know, the gods the Greeks worshiped, the myths they told, and the great athletic festival that, every four years, briefly united a divided people in peace.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Greek philosophy began with thinkers who sought natural rather than mythical explanations, but it reached its height in Athens with three linked figures. Socrates (about 470 to 399 BCE) wrote nothing himself; he questioned his fellow citizens relentlessly about virtue and knowledge, and was executed in 399 BCE for allegedly corrupting the youth. His student Plato (about 428 to 348 BCE) founded the Academy and wrote dialogues arguing that reality lies in perfect Forms beyond the senses. Plato's student Aristotle (384 to 322 BCE) founded the Lyceum, studied everything from logic to biology, and tutored Alexander the Great. Greek religion was polytheistic, centered on the Twelve Olympians led by Zeus and dwelling on Mount Olympus. People consulted oracles, above all the Pythia at Delphi, and told rich myths of gods and heroes. Religion and athletics joined at the Olympic Games, first recorded in 776 BCE and held every four years at Olympia in honor of Zeus, during which a sacred truce paused wars so athletes could compete.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: Socrates (about 470 to 399 BCE): the questioning philosopher who left no writings and was sentenced to drink hemlock in 399 BCE. Plato (about 428 to 348 BCE): his student, founder of the Academy and author of dialogues such as the Republic, famous for the theory of Forms and the allegory of the cave. Aristotle (384 to 322 BCE): Plato's student, founder of the Lyceum, a systematic thinker across logic, ethics, politics, and natural science, and the tutor of Alexander. The Twelve Olympians: Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes, Demeter, and Dionysus (lists vary slightly). Oracle of Delphi: the shrine of Apollo where the priestess, the Pythia, delivered prophecies. Olympic Games: first recorded in 776 BCE, held every four years at Olympia; a sacred truce protected travelers and competitors. The clean chain to remember is teacher to student: Socrates taught Plato, and Plato taught Aristotle.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Put Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle in order of teacher to student. 2) Which philosopher wrote nothing himself and was executed in 399 BCE? 3) What did Plato call the perfect, unchanging realities behind appearances? 4) Whom did Aristotle tutor? 5) Who was the king of the Twelve Olympian gods, and where did they dwell? 6) In which year were the Olympic Games traditionally first held, and how often were they staged? Answers: 1) Socrates taught Plato, who taught Aristotle. 2) Socrates. 3) The Forms. 4) Alexander the Great. 5) Zeus, on Mount Olympus. 6) 776 BCE, every four years.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reversing the teaching chain. It runs Socrates to Plato to Aristotle, oldest to youngest. Mistake: thinking Socrates left books; he wrote nothing, and we know him mainly through Plato's dialogues. Mistake: confusing the schools; Plato founded the Academy, Aristotle the Lyceum. Mistake: treating Greek religion as having one god; it was polytheistic, with the Twelve Olympians and countless local cults, and the Olympic Games were a religious festival for Zeus, not merely a sporting event. One more caution: the Pythia at Delphi spoke for Apollo, not Zeus, though Zeus was king of the gods. Exit ticket: (a) Which philosopher tutored Alexander the Great? (b) In what year were the first Olympic Games held, and to which god were they dedicated? Answers: (a) Aristotle. (b) 776 BCE, dedicated to Zeus.

items.translation: an independent Greek city-state with its own laws, army, and gods
items.example: Athens and Sparta were the two most powerful examples of the Greek polis.

items.translation: rule by the people; in Athens, direct voting by free adult male citizens
items.example: Cleisthenes helped establish democracy in Athens in 508 BCE.

items.translation: a heavily armed Greek citizen-soldier who fought in a shield wall called a phalanx
items.example: Rows of hoplites locked their shields to form a phalanx at Marathon.

items.translation: a sacred site, or its priest, through which a god was believed to answer questions; the most famous was at Delphi
items.example: Before war, leaders often sent to the oracle at Delphi for advice.

items.translation: describing the Greek-influenced culture that spread across the Near East after Alexander the Great
items.example: The Hellenistic age blended Greek and Eastern ideas from Egypt to India.

items.translation: literally the love of wisdom; the Greek pursuit of reasoned answers about knowledge, nature, and how to live
items.example: Socrates turned philosophy toward questions of virtue and the good life.

questions.explanation: The Parthenon on the Acropolis honored Athena, patron goddess of Athens.

questions.explanation: Pericles dominated Athenian politics from about 461 to 429 BCE and drove the building program.

questions.prompt: Which historian wrote a rigorous account of the Peloponnesian War?
questions.explanation: Thucydides wrote the eyewitness history of the war; Herodotus covered the Persian Wars.

questions.explanation: Socrates taught Plato, and Plato taught Aristotle.

questions.explanation: The Pythia at Delphi was the oracle of Apollo.

questions.explanation: The first recorded games were in 776 BCE, held every four years at Olympia.

lessons.title: The Peloponnesian War, Alexander, and the Hellenistic legacy
lessons.grammar_note: Rome did not erase Greek culture but adopted it, which is why Greek words and ideas survive in modern law, science, and government.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how the Greek city-states exhausted themselves, how Macedon and Alexander the Great transformed the Greek world, and why Greek civilization still shapes ours. By the end you will be able to summarize the Peloponnesian War and its outcome, trace Alexander's conquests and the Hellenistic kingdoms that followed, and list the lasting legacies of Greece in politics, thought, science, and art. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which two city-states fought the Peloponnesian War, and from which kingdom did Alexander come? Keep both answers ready. This final lesson carries the story from the self-inflicted decline of the classical poleis through the brief, dazzling empire of Alexander to the long afterlife of Greek ideas, an afterlife we still live inside every time we vote, reason, or measure the world.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The Golden Age ended in a long civil war. The Peloponnesian War (431 to 404 BCE) pitted Athens and its naval empire against Sparta and its land-based alliance. A plague struck Athens in 430 BCE and killed Pericles in 429 BCE; a disastrous Athenian expedition to Sicily (415 to 413 BCE) wrecked its fleet; and in 404 BCE Athens surrendered. Sparta's dominance did not last, and decades of infighting left all the poleis weak, as when Thebes broke Spartan power at Leuctra in 371 BCE. Into this exhaustion stepped Macedon to the north. King Philip II mastered Greece at the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE, and his son Alexander the Great (356 to 323 BCE) then conquered the Persian Empire, winning at Granicus, Issus, and Gaugamela and reaching India before dying at Babylon in 323 BCE. His generals carved his realm into the Hellenistic kingdoms, spreading Greek language and culture across the Near East until Rome absorbed them, taking Egypt in 30 BCE.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: Peloponnesian War (431 to 404 BCE): Athens versus Sparta, chronicled by Thucydides. Plague of Athens (430 BCE): an epidemic that killed perhaps a third of the city, including Pericles in 429 BCE. Sicilian Expedition (415 to 413 BCE): Athens's catastrophic attack on Syracuse. Athenian surrender (404 BCE): the end of its empire. Battle of Leuctra (371 BCE): Thebes, under Epaminondas, shattered Spartan supremacy. Philip II of Macedon: unified Greece after the Battle of Chaeronea (338 BCE). Alexander the Great (356 to 323 BCE): conquered Persia (Granicus 334, Issus 333, Gaugamela 331 BCE) and reached India before dying at Babylon in 323 BCE. Hellenistic kingdoms: the Ptolemaic, Seleucid, and Antigonid states founded by his successors, home to the Library of Alexandria and to scientists such as Euclid, Archimedes, and Eratosthenes. Rome absorbed the Greek world over the following centuries, ending with Ptolemaic Egypt in 30 BCE.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which two city-states fought the Peloponnesian War, and in what years? 2) What disaster struck Athens in 430 BCE and helped kill Pericles? 3) In which 338 BCE battle did Philip II master Greece? 4) Name two of the three great battles by which Alexander defeated Persia. 5) Name one Hellenistic kingdom. 6) Name one Greek scientist of the Hellenistic age. Answers: 1) Athens and Sparta, 431 to 404 BCE. 2) A plague, which killed Pericles in 429 BCE. 3) The Battle of Chaeronea. 4) Any two of Granicus, Issus, and Gaugamela. 5) The Ptolemaic, Seleucid, or Antigonid kingdom. 6) Euclid, Archimedes, or Eratosthenes.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking a foreign power beat the classical poleis. The Peloponnesian War was a Greek civil war that Athens and Sparta inflicted on themselves, leaving all the city-states weak enough for Macedon to dominate. Mistake: confusing Philip and Alexander; Philip II unified Greece at Chaeronea in 338 BCE, and his son Alexander then conquered Persia. Mistake: dating Alexander's death wrongly; he died young at Babylon in 323 BCE, and his generals divided the empire. Mistake: assuming Greek culture ended with Roman conquest; instead Rome absorbed and spread it, which is why Greek democracy, philosophy, science, drama, and art reached the modern world. Exit ticket: (a) Who won the Peloponnesian War, and in what year did Athens surrender? (b) Name two lasting legacies of ancient Greece. Answers: (a) Sparta; Athens surrendered in 404 BCE. (b) Any two of democracy, philosophy, science, mathematics, drama, and classical art and architecture.
